What Is the Web Frontend?

The frontend is the part of a web application you see and use in the browser.

HTML

Defines the content and structure of the page.

CSS

Controls its visual appearance and layout.

JavaScript

Runs code that handles actions and updates the interface.

The frontend can request data such as stock prices from a server.

What Is HTML?

HTML describes the content and structure of a web page.

  • HTML stands for HyperText Markup Language.
  • Hypertext connects documents or sections through links.
  • A markup language uses tags to mark headings, paragraphs, and other parts of a document.
  • An HTML document combines tags and content. The browser reads it and displays a web page.

HTML Tags and Elements

  • Tag. Markup in the source that starts or ends an element. In the figure, <p class="nice"> is the opening tag and </p> is the closing tag.
  • Element. A unit of the page’s structure. Here, the opening tag, the text Hello world!, and the closing tag together define one paragraph element.

The class attribute and its value are part of the opening tag. Void elements such as <img> have no closing tag.

MF20006 / HTML and CSS10 / 55

A Complete HTML Document

<title> names the browser tab. <h1> appears inside the page.

MF20006 / HTML and CSS11 / 55

Four Basic HTML Tags

  • Heading
    <h1>World Trade</h1>

    h1 marks the highest heading level. World Trade is the heading text. Use h2–h6 for lower levels.

  • Paragraph
    <p>Compare economies.</p>

    p marks a paragraph. The text between the two tags is the paragraph’s content.

  • Link
    <a href="trade.html">Trade data</a>

    href sets the destination to trade.html. Trade data is the text readers click.

  • Image
    <img src="trade.png" alt="Trade chart">

    src points to the image file. alt gives its text alternative. img has no closing tag.

MF20006 / HTML and CSS20 / 55

What Is CSS?

CSS stands for Cascading Style Sheets.

What CSS describes
  • Typography and color. Set font size, line height, and text color.
  • Boxes and spacing. Add backgrounds, borders, padding, and margins.
  • Layout. Arrange cards in rows or build a page with columns.
  • Responsive design. Stack those columns on a narrow screen.
  • Interaction states. Highlight a link on hover or an input on keyboard focus.
  • Motion. Fade an element in or make a color change gradual.
How CSS works with HTML
  • HTML describes the content and structure of a page.
  • CSS rules describe how that content looks and where it appears.
  • One rule can apply to many elements. One stylesheet can apply to many pages.
MF20006 / HTML and CSS21 / 55

CSS Rule Syntax

Read a CSS rule by finding what it matches and what it changes.

A declaration pairs a property with a value. Braces enclose declarations, a colon separates the property and value, and semicolons separate declarations.
One CSS rule
.metric {
  color: red;
}

Match this selector to the HTML attribute class="metric".

Parts of the rule
Selector · .metric
Matches elements with the class metric.
Property · color
Chooses what to change, here the text color.
Value · red
Sets the new color.
MF20006 / HTML and CSS22 / 55

CSS ID and Class Selectors

A selector tells the browser which HTML elements a rule applies to.

  • ID selector #para1

    Use # followed by an ID. This matches the element with id="para1". Each ID should appear once per page.

  • Class selector .center

    Use . followed by a class name. This matches every element with class="center". Several elements can share a class.

  • Class on a specific tag p.center

    Put the tag name directly before the class selector. This matches only <p> elements with the center class.

MF20006 / HTML and CSS23 / 55

Adding CSS to HTML

  • External stylesheet
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="styles.css">

    Put the rule in styles.css and put the <link> in <head>. Multiple pages can load the same file.

  • Internal stylesheet
    <style>
  .metric { color: green; margin-left: 16px; }
</style>

    Write a rule in <style> in the <head>. Here it sets color and margin-left.

  • Inline style
    <p style="color: purple; font-weight: bold;">Imports</p>

    Write declarations in the element’s style attribute. Here it sets color and font-weight.

  • One property at a time: CSS decides which declaration wins for each property separately.
  • Inline vs. stylesheet: Normally, inline styles take precedence over internal and external CSS.
  • Internal vs. external: Neither automatically wins. More specific selectors take precedence. If specificity is equal, the later declaration wins.
MF20006 / HTML and CSS24 / 55

The CSS Box Model

Every HTML element occupies a rectangular box. The box model explains its size and the space around it.

Think of a product card: the product description is the content; empty space around the words is padding; the visible outline is the border; space separating this card from other cards is the margin.
From the inside out
Margin · outside spacing
Border · visible edge
Padding · inside spacing
Content · text / image
Remember: Padding is inside the border; margin is outside it. Margin is transparent and does not paint the element's background.
Examples · Change one property at a time
PRODUCT
CONTENT
■ Margin (orange)■ Border (blue)■ Padding (green)■ Content (white)
.summary {
  width: 140px;
  padding: 12px;
  border: 4px solid #2266ac;
  margin: 16px;
}

Visible width = 172px (content + padding × 2 + border × 2). Margin stays outside.

Chapter 2

JavaScript and the DOM

MF20006 / JavaScript and the DOM26 / 55

What Is JavaScript?

JavaScript is a programming language. In the browser, it can read data, run instructions, and respond to user actions.

What can it do?

  • Respond to actions. Run code when a user clicks a button, types, or changes a selection.
  • Update the page. Change text, show details, or switch between a table and a chart.
  • Process data. Calculate a percentage change, sort values, or filter a list.
  • Check input. Check whether a quantity meets a rule and display a helpful message.
  • Request data. Load information from a server and display it in the page.
MF20006 / JavaScript and the DOM27 / 55

Using JavaScript in HTML

The browser reads HTML from top to bottom and builds the DOM as it goes.

A script that uses a page element must run after that element has been parsed. Script attributes control when it runs.
  • Regular external script
    <script src="app.js"></script>

    The HTML parser pauses while the script loads and runs, then continues. Place it after the elements it needs.

  • Deferred external script
    <script src="app.js" defer></script>

    defer allows loading during HTML parsing. Execution waits until parsing is complete. Deferred scripts run in document order.

  • External module script
    <script type="module" src="app.js"></script>

    With type="module", the browser waits until all HTML has been parsed before running the JavaScript module.

Inline JavaScript goes between <script> and </script>. A module needs no defer. These examples use no async attribute.

MF20006 / JavaScript and the DOM28 / 55

Values and Variables

Common JavaScript Data Types

String
Text, such as "AAPL".
Number
Numeric values, including integers such as 190 and fractional values such as 1.2.
Boolean
true or false.
Undefined
A value not yet assigned, such as let result;.
Null
An intentional empty value. The only value of this type is null.
Object
Structured data, such as { price: 190 }. Arrays are objects too.
JavaScript
const symbol = "AAPL";
const price = 190;
let quantity = 2;
const saved = false;

quantity = quantity + 1;
const total = price * quantity;
How to read it
  • const creates a binding that cannot be reassigned.
  • let allows reassignment.
  • Quotes enclose a string. Numbers can be used in calculations. true and false are booleans.
  • = assigns a value. Here total becomes 570.

Objects and Arrays

Use an object for one stock and an array for several stocks.

JavaScript
const stock = {
  symbol: "AAPL",
  price: 190,
  change: 1.2
};
const stocks = [stock];

stock.price = 191;
const symbol = stocks[0].symbol;
How to read it
  • An object contains properties. Here symbol, price, and change are property names. stock.price reads the price value.
  • An array groups items in order. Index 0 is the first item.
  • const keeps the variable bound to the same object or array. Its contents can still change: update a property with stock.price = 191, or add an array item with stocks.push(stock).

MF20006 / JavaScript and the DOM30 / 55

Functions and Callbacks

A function groups instructions. A callback runs when something happens.

JavaScript
function total(price, quantity) {
  return price * quantity;
}
const amount = total(190, 3);

button.addEventListener("click", () => {
  message.textContent = amount;
});
How to read it
  • price and quantity are parameters.
  • total(190, 3) calls the function.
  • return supplies the result.
  • Arrow function. (parameters) => { … } defines a function. () means no parameters are declared; the braces contain the instructions. Here, addEventListener registers the function, and the browser calls it on a click.
    A short form such as n => n * 2 returns the expression automatically.

Edit example opens a small runnable version of this idea.

MF20006 / JavaScript and the DOM31 / 55

Conditions and Early Returns

Use a condition to decide which instructions run.

JavaScript
function describe(change) {
  if (change > 0) {
    return "Gainer";
  }
  if (change < 0) {
    return "Loser";
  }
  return "Unchanged";
}
How to read it
  • if checks a condition.
  • > and < compare values.
  • == allows type conversion when comparing values; === compares without type conversion. For example, 5 == "5" is true, while 5 === "5" is false.
  • return ends this function call.

Edit example opens a small runnable version of this idea.

MF20006 / JavaScript and the DOM33 / 55

How Can JavaScript Reach HTML?

A click should change this heading. How does the script find the right element?

HTML and JavaScript
<h1 id="page-title">World Trade</h1>
<button id="update">Change title</button>

// JavaScript
const heading = document.getElementById("page-title");
const button = document.getElementById("update");

button.addEventListener("click", () => {
  heading.textContent = "Trade Overview";
});
Try the button
  • document is the browser-provided object representing the current page. It is the entry point for finding and updating elements.
  • The id identifies the heading.
  • document.getElementById() returns the matching element.
  • Setting textContent updates its text in the page.

The browser provides a model of the page and APIs to work with it. We call this the Document Object Model (DOM).

MF20006 / JavaScript and the DOM34 / 55

What Is the DOM?

DOM stands for Document Object Model.

document represents the document node. The browser builds a tree containing the html, head, and body elements.
HTML source
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <title>MarketLab</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <main id="content">
      <h1 id="page-title">World Trade</h1>
      <p>Compare <a href="markets.html">markets</a>.</p>
    </main>
  </body>
</html>
DOM tree
#document
├─ <!DOCTYPE html>
└─ html
   ├─ head
   │  ├─ meta
   │  └─ title
   │     └─ #text "MarketLab"
   └─ body
      └─ main#content
         ├─ h1#page-title
         │  └─ #text "World Trade"
         └─ p
            ├─ #text "Compare "
            ├─ a [href="markets.html"]
            │  └─ #text "markets"
            └─ #text "."

Elements and text are nodes. Attributes belong to elements. Whitespace-only text nodes are omitted here.

MF20006 / JavaScript and the DOM35 / 55

Read the Search Input

Type a ticker. JavaScript reads the input before the stock list is refreshed.

JavaScript excerpt
const find = id => document.getElementById(id);

find('search').addEventListener('input', event => {
  state.q = event.target.value.trim();
  renderMarketActions();
  clearTimeout(debounce);
  debounce = setTimeout(resetList, 140);
});
DOM operations to follow
  • find('search') finds <input id="search"> through document.getElementById().
  • addEventListener('input', ...) responds as the user edits the field.
  • event.target.value reads the current text. trim() removes outer whitespace.
  • state.q stores the query. The timer schedules the list refresh after 140 ms.
MF20006 / JavaScript and the DOM36 / 55

Star a Stock

Click the star beside a stock. JavaScript updates the watchlist and the button.

JavaScript excerpt
find('detail-watch').addEventListener('click', () => {
  if (state.selected) updateWatch(state.selected);
});

// Selected lines from renderDetail()
const picked = state.saved.has(stock.id);
find('detail-watch').textContent =
  picked ? '★' : '☆';
find('detail-watch').setAttribute(
  'aria-pressed', String(picked));
DOM operations to follow
  • find('detail-watch') selects the star button by its HTML id.
  • addEventListener('click', ...) calls updateWatch() for the selected stock.
  • state.saved.has(stock.id) checks whether that stock is saved. The update adds or removes it, then redraws the controls.
  • textContent changes ☆ to ★. aria-pressed records the button’s selected state.
MF20006 / JavaScript and the DOM37 / 55

Draw Price History

JavaScript reads historical prices and draws a line inside the HTML canvas element.

JavaScript excerpt
const canvas = find('chart');
const context = canvas.getContext('2d');

// Selected drawing steps from drawChart()
context.beginPath();
context.moveTo(x(0), y(points[0].price));
for (let i = 1; i < points.length; i++)
  context.lineTo(x(i), y(points[i].price));
context.strokeStyle = '#7fb6ff';
context.lineWidth = 2;
context.stroke();
DOM operations to follow
  • find('chart') selects <canvas id="chart">. getContext('2d') provides its drawing API.
  • state.points holds dated prices. In drawChart(), x(i) and y(price) convert them into canvas coordinates.
  • beginPath() starts the line. moveTo() sets its first point, lineTo() adds points, and stroke() draws it.
  • The curve consists of pixels inside one DOM element. loadChart() supplies the data and calls drawChart().

JSON: Data in the Response

JSON means JavaScript Object Notation. It is a text format for exchanging structured data.

Example JSON response
{
  "range": "1M",
  "points": [
    { "date": "2026-11-10", "price": 225 },
    { "date": "2026-11-11", "price": 228 }
  ]
}
Reading the example
  • { } contains an object. Each property has a name and a value, such as "range": "1M".
  • [ ] contains an array. Each item in points holds a date and a price.
  • JSON property names and strings use double quotes. JSON contains data, with no functions or comments.
  • await response.json() parses the body into a JavaScript value. Then data.points[0].price reads 225.
MF20006 / Ajax and Fetch41 / 55

What Is Ajax?

Ajax lets a page exchange data with the server and update part of its content without loading a whole new page.

  • The name: Ajax stands for Asynchronous JavaScript and XML.
  • Asynchronous: The browser can handle other work while the request is pending.
  • Partial updates: A new price series can replace the chart while the search field and toolbar stay in place.
  • Data format: Ajax can use JSON or other formats. The historical name includes XML, but XML is optional.
  • Implementation: Earlier code commonly used XMLHttpRequest. Today, fetch() is a common way to implement this interaction.
MF20006 / Ajax and Fetch42 / 55

Before Ajax: Loading a New Page

In the traditional model, following a link or submitting a form loads a complete page from the server.

1

Browser sends a request

A link or form starts navigation, such as asking for the 1M price history.

2

Server builds the page

Backend code gets the data and prepares a complete HTML document.

3

Server returns HTML

The response contains the page structure and the updated content.

4

Browser loads the page

The new document replaces the previous one, including unchanged parts.

Response: a complete HTML document

<!doctype html>
<html>
  <head><title>Price history</title></head>
  <body>
    <header>Stock Explorer</header>
    <main>Updated price history...</main>
  </body>
</html>

How Ajax Works

JavaScript requests data in the background, then updates the relevant part of the current page.

1

User triggers an event

A click or input event starts JavaScript code in the current page.

2

JavaScript requests data

Fetch or XMLHttpRequest sends an HTTP request without navigating away.

3

Server returns data

The response often contains JSON. The page can remain interactive while waiting.

4

JavaScript updates the page

Read the response, then change DOM content or redraw the canvas.

Response: data for the update

{
  "range": "1M",
  "points": [
    { "date": "2026-11-10", "price": 225 },
    { "date": "2026-11-11", "price": 228 }
  ]
}

MF20006 / Ajax and Fetch44 / 55

Fetch: Requesting Data with JavaScript

fetch(url, options) starts a request. With no method option, it uses GET.

JavaScript
async function readHistory() {
  const url =
    '/api/history?id=AAPL%3AXNAS&range=1M';
  const response = await fetch(url);
  const data = await response.json();
  return data.points;
}
Reading the example
  • url identifies the resource. The optional options object configures settings such as the method and headers.
  • fetch() returns a Promise, representing a result that may become available later.
  • async allows await inside this function. await fetch(url) pauses this function until a Response is available.
  • await response.json() reads and parses the body. The next page adds response checks and failure handling.
MF20006 / Ajax and Fetch45 / 55

Checking the Response and Handling Errors

A response may report an HTTP error. The network request or JSON parsing may also fail.

JavaScript
async function readHistory(url) {
  try {
    const response = await fetch(url);
    if (!response.ok)
      throw new Error('HTTP ' + response.status);
    const data = await response.json();
    return data;
  } catch (error) {
    showStatus(error.message);
  }
}
Reading the example
  • response.status contains the HTTP status code. response.ok is true for status codes 200–299.
  • fetch() can fulfill even for 404 or 500. Check ok explicitly.
  • throw new Error(...) turns an unsuccessful HTTP status into a failure that catch can handle.
  • try...catch handles thrown HTTP errors, network failures and invalid JSON. showStatus() is our page-update helper.

Why Do We Need Frontend Frameworks?

Question: When you save one stock, how many parts of the page must change?

After one click: Save AAPL

Stock ExplorerWatchlist: 1

MSFT $435 ☆ Save

Stock detail · AAPL

$190

★ Saved

Both buttons, the watchlist and navigation now depend on the same saved state.

What if we add more watchlist features?

A saved-only view, sector summary or quick-access menu adds more UI updates to coordinate.

Vanilla JavaScript · update flow
function saveStock(stock) {
  state.saved.set(stock.id, stock);
  renderStockList();    // list button
  renderStockDetail();  // detail button
  renderWatchlist();
  renderNavigation();   // badge and menu

  // More features, more views to update:
  renderSavedOnlyView();
  renderSectorSummary();
  renderQuickAccessMenu();
}

Each render... function reads shared state and updates a dependent area.

Without a framework, manually coordinating these updates becomes harder to maintain as features grow.

MF20006 / Modern Frontend Frameworks51 / 55

Declarative UI and State Updates

The same saved state can drive the same button. The difference is how the developer describes the update.

Vanilla JavaScript
const button = document.getElementById("watch-native");
const output = document.getElementById("native-state");
let saved = false;
button.addEventListener("click", () => {
  saved = !saved;
  button.textContent = saved ? "★" : "☆";
  output.textContent = "saved: " + saved;
});
saved: false

Find the DOM element and explicitly change its content.

React · JSX
function WatchButton() {
  const [saved, setSaved] = React.useState(false);
  return <div>
    <button onClick={() => setSaved(!saved)}>
      {saved ? "★" : "☆"}
    </button>
    <output>saved: {String(saved)}</output>
  </div>;
}

useState(false) creates state. setSaved() schedules its update. The JSX describes what to show.

Frameworks and UI Libraries

These technologies share UI ideas, while offering different syntax and different amounts of application infrastructure.

React

UI library

Supported by Meta and the community. Components, JSX, Hooks and a broad ecosystem.

Example fit: a data-rich dashboard.

Template / JSX style
<StockCard price={190} />

Vue

Progressive framework

Templates and a reactivity system. Can be adopted gradually in an existing site.

Example fit: an existing site or a full web app.

Template / JSX style
<StockCard :price="190" />

Angular

Application framework

TypeScript-based components and integrated capabilities such as dependency injection.

Example fit: a large, structured application.

Template / JSX style
<stock-card [price]="190" />

Svelte

Compiler-based UI framework

Compiles component code, reducing work that must happen at runtime.

Example fit: a component-based interactive app.

Template / JSX style
<StockCard price={190} />

Ajax and Frameworks Work Together

Fetch retrieves data. The framework uses component state to organize the interface and its updates.

  1. ClickThe user chooses Refresh price.
  2. FetchJavaScript requests data.
  3. JSONThe response represents the price.
  4. StatesetPrice(data.price) updates state.
  5. FrameworkReact coordinates the UI update.
  6. DOMThe browser shows the new price.
Inside a React component
async function refreshPrice() {
  const response = await fetch(sampleURL);
  if (!response.ok) throw new Error("Request failed");
  const data = await response.json();
  setPrice(data.price);
}

sampleURL contains local JSON. The example simulates a response and keeps the page open.
